summary: Gives an overview, threat analysis and requirements for the Keying and Authentication for Routing Protocols effort. Existing authentication methods in routing protocols are often dated, vulnerable or use deprecated algorithms, and KARP aims to improve them. It is informational.

eli5.summary: The secret handshakes routers use are old and easy to fake. This lays out the problems and what new, stronger handshakes must do.

questions: how to secure routing protocol authentication
why routing protocol authentication is weak
subtitle: Securing how routers talk to each other

tldr.problem: Routing protocols like BGP and OSPF use outdated authentication methods that are vulnerable to attacks, employ deprecated cryptography, and are operationally burdensome to maintain. Attackers can spoof routers or intercept routing updates, destabilizing the network.
tldr.mechanism: KARP is a multi-year effort to overhaul routing protocol security. This RFC catalogs the threats, defines which are in scope (spoofing, tampering, unauthorized key holders), and establishes requirements for protocol updates: stronger algorithms, efficient rekeying, backward compatibility, and deployability on existing hardware.
tldr.outcome: The RFC provides a roadmap for working groups to improve each routing protocol incrementally, starting with updates to existing mechanisms (Phase 1) and moving toward automated key management (Phase 2). Success is measured by operator deployment.

facts.label: Scope
facts.value: Message authentication and integrity for routing protocols

facts.label: Phase 1 focus
facts.value: Updates to existing transport security mechanisms

today: RFC 6862 is Informational and serves as the threat and requirements document for the KARP working group effort. It remains the foundation for routing protocol security improvements, with TCP-AO for BGP, HMAC-SHA for OSPF, and similar upgrades to other routing protocols following its guidance.

sections.title: Why Routing Protocols Need Better Security
sections.content:
The routing system is critical infrastructure: if routers are attacked and forced to share false routing information, large parts of the Internet can become unreachable or send traffic to the wrong place. The IAB workshop in 2006 identified routing as a target of minimal cost but maximal disruption.

Most routing protocols (BGP, OSPF, IS-IS, RIP) already have some authentication, but the mechanisms are often dated (like TCP MD5 from 1997), use deprecated algorithms (like MD5), or employ weak cryptography. Field surveys show that operators often use the same key for years (sometimes five or more years without changes), use one key for the entire network, and change keys only rarely because rekeying causes routing adjacencies to bounce.

KARP aims to overhaul these mechanisms, moving from current practice to modern cryptography, while staying deployable on existing routers without unacceptable performance penalties.
sections.eli5: Routers use passwords from 1997 to check that they are talking to the right neighbor. Those passwords are old and weak, and changing them is a pain that breaks the network temporarily.

sections.title: Threats to Routing Protocols
sections.content:
KARP focuses on three threat sources:

OUTSIDERS are attackers outside the routing domain who want to disrupt it. On-path outsiders (like a man-in-the-middle attacker) can tamper with packets between routers. Off-path outsiders can spoof router addresses and inject false routing data.

Unauthorized Key Holders are people who should not have the authentication keys but do. An employee who leaves the company but retains a copy of the key can impersonate routers. An attacker who steals keys from one router can use them to spoof its peers.

BYZANTINE routers are legitimate routers that are faulty, misconfigured, or compromised and send bogus routing information. KARP does not address Byzantine failures, which require different defense mechanisms.

KARP is explicitly out of scope for sniffing (passive eavesdropping), message delays, non-repudiation, and attacks from within the routing protocol's own source (faulty data announced by a real router).
sections.eli5: There are three kinds of bad guys: strangers on the network who want to fake being a router, people who have stolen the password, and broken routers that send false information. KARP stops the first two but not the broken router.

sections.title: Modernizing Authentication
sections.content:
KARP Phase 1 updates existing mechanisms (like TCP-AO for BGP). Requirements include:

Cryptography: Use strong, modern algorithms from IETF-approved sources. Do not invent new algorithms. Support algorithm agility: the ability to switch algorithms without protocol redesign, because algorithms break over time.

Key management: Support pre-shared keys (for operational simplicity) and be ready for automated key management later. Avoid long-lived keys by supporting frequent rekeying without disrupting routing sessions. Rekeying must work even when a key is only known to one peer initially.

Replay protection: Block attackers from resending old messages from the same session (intra-session) or from an earlier session (inter-session). This must work even when the router prioritizes certain packets.

Deployment: Work incrementally, without requiring all routers to update at once. Support both secured and unsecured routers operating together. Provide clear defaults so implementations work without extensive configuration. Minimize CPU impact on existing hardware.
sections.eli5: New methods need modern passwords instead of old ones, ways to change passwords without breaking routing, and the ability to do it one router at a time without forcing all routers to update together.

sections.title: Incremental, Realistic Improvements
sections.content:
KARP acknowledges that perfect security comes second to operational reality. Deployed routers have been tuned over 20 years and cannot support the most advanced cryptography without performance penalties. Therefore, KARP uses a 'crawl, walk, run' approach.

Early updates to a protocol may use 'SHOULD' language for enhanced features (meaning 'try this if you can') with the intention that the same feature becomes 'MUST' in a future release. This gives vendors and operators time to optimize implementations.

For example, TCP-AO for BGP initially addressed algorithm agility and replay protection without specifying a full key management protocol. Key management came later.

The RFC recognizes that operators value performance and service availability. Convergence times (how fast a network recovers after a link fails) must not degrade by more than 5%. Rekeying must not cause routing adjacencies to drop, which would take customer circuits offline.
sections.eli5: You do not have to be perfect all at once. Start with security that is much better than today, run tests on the hardware to make sure it does not break, then improve it more in future versions.

sections.title: Future Automated Key Management
sections.content:
KARP Phase 2 (not in this RFC) will address automated key management protocols (KMPs). Today, keys are often distributed manually, which is error-prone and slow. An automated KMP would negotiate keys between routers without manual intervention.

Automated key management is critical to solving the terminated-employee problem: when staff leaves, keys must be revoked immediately and new ones deployed to all routers quickly. Manual processes cannot do this fast enough or easily enough.

The RFC requires Phase 1 updates to support eventual KMP integration, without forcing KMP use initially. This lets operators deploy better authentication now while preparing for automated key management later. Manual keying must always remain supported for backward compatibility.
sections.eli5: Someday, routers will ask each other for new passwords automatically, like two friends texting a new meeting time. For now, an administrator types the password on each router.
